newsitem.title: BELGIUM: European shops fight bank card charges.
newsitem.headline: European shops fight bank card charges.

text.p: Retailers united forces on Thursday to urge the European Union to scrap rules allowing banks to impose 'excessive' charges on shops and restaurants for accepting payment cards.
At issue is a so-called non-discrimination rule (NDR) which says that merchants, not cardholders, bear transaction costs so that credit and debit cards are treated the same way as cash.

The result, says EuroCommerce, which represents retail, wholesale and international trade in the Union, is that all consumers end up paying because shops have no choice but to add the charges to the final price.

"Not only merchants suffer, non-cardholding customers (the cash payers) equally subsidise the system because merchants generally had to raise their prices to recuperate at least part of the charges," it said in a statement.

In a formal complaint to the European Commission about the charges, EuroCommerce argued that if the NDR rule was scrapped it would probably result in a reduction of card charges as banks would not want to lose business.
Experience in Britain, Sweden and the Netherlands, where the rule was made illegal, also proved cardholders would not automatically lose out.
Citing the example of Sweden, Eurocommerce said:

"Once merchants could not be forced anymore to pay the card usage costs, competition between banks started working, with the effect that the price of the card usage went down, for some cards to zero, and card usage in general went further up."
Banks argue that cards must not be discriminated against and invoke the consumers' right to know how much they are going to pay for goods and services, not being surprised with hefty commissions.
In Britain credit card holders are not charged even though the rule was suppressed in 1989.

The spokesman for European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert said in February that the Commission would like the rule to disappear allowing for more transparent costs and giving retailers greater leverage on the banking system.
But Van Miert's competition service is having problems explaining to the rest of the Commission why it should take a decision which could be seen as potentially harmful for consumers.
The European consumer organisation BEUC is split over the issue.

The Commission's objections only apply to NDR and would leave untouched the so-called multilateral interchange fee (MIS) paid by a shop's bank to the cardholder's bank for its involvement in a transaction. This fee is ultimately paid by the shops.

Besides the price paid for processing card payments, retailers must also pay an ad valorem fee, which depends on the transactions carried out with cards. Eurocommerce has estimated that total charges paid by stores and restaurants vary between less than one percent and five percent of sales.
